title: MUX: Continuous Reasoning via Multiplexed Tokens
claim: Supervise each continuous latent token with a position-weighted superposition of a discrete reasoning span, using local distillation losses.
layout: Single panel; bottom-up LLM flow, top span targets, left weighting menu
description: A single wide diagram. At the bottom, a green Large Language Model bar takes three inputs: a Question (teal tokens), Continuous reasoning (dark tokens x1…xK between <bot> and <eot>), and an Answer (blue tokens). Arrows lead up to output latent tokens x1…xK and blue answer tokens. An arrow from token x_i points up to a dark bar chart over a vocabulary (+ a 3 z 5 0 8 =). At the top, pink reasoning spans r1…rM contain tokens such as 5 + 3 = 8. Those tokens connect to purple bars of decreasing height, labeled Multiplexing. The bars merge into a target distribution. A bracket labeled L_local links prediction and target. A blue bracket labeled L_answer covers the answer tokens. At left, three boxes offer positional weightings (Geometric highlighted, Sinusoidal and Rotational greyed out). The eye goes first to the colorful top spans and the central bar charts.
caption: Overview of \ours. Given a question, the language model predicts a sequence of continuous latent reasoning tokens. Each token is linearly projected to the vocabulary space and is trained to represent a local span of discrete reasoning steps. We construct the learning target from each discrete span as a weighted average of one-hot encodings, and train each latent token with local KL divergence loss. The answer is trained with standard cross-entropy loss.
abstract: Language models solve complex problems by articulating intermediate reasoning steps in natural language. While effective, this process is computationally bottlenecked: each reasoning step conveys only a single subword, and many are spent expressing a thought instead of carrying out computation. We propose MUX, a simple method for high-bandwidth and compact reasoning based on distillation of discrete reasoning into continuous multiplexed tokens in a latent space. Here, each latent token is trained to represent a weighted linear superposition (multiplexing) of a span of discrete reasoning subwords, where this superposition is lossless by construction and the span can be fully recovered (demultiplexing). We prove that simple position-dependent weightings, such as suitable geometric decay, support lossless multiplexing, which in turn prevents shortcut behaviors caused by latent collapse. We further show that multiplexed reasoning can perform parallel exploration in problems that require search. Across 32 evaluation settings spanning four language models, MUX outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines. Ablation and probing analyses further show that the learned latent tokens encode faithful and interpretable reasoning. Our results suggest that lossless superposition as local learning targets constitutes a sufficient condition for achieving strong and efficient latent continuous reasoning.
